name: Heather
lede: Heather is the dusty purple of the moorland shrub's flowers, a muted mauve-grey that is more a texture than a single hue.

sections.title: A speckled color
sections.body:
Paterson defines heather as the speckled purplish-grey-blue of the plant [1], and the French *bruyère* as a greyish purple of heather [2]. St Clair adds that before the twentieth century the word was a synonym for mottled, and that it now means a pinkish purple [3]. The speckle is the point: a hillside of heather is many small flowers, not one flat color.

The same idea runs through wool. In a Scottish tweed maker's account, Finlay finds heather purple among the colors built into the body of a formal jacket, alongside candy pink and sun yellow [4]. For the fabric sense, see [[heather-grey]].

sections.title: Neighbors
sections.body: Heather sits near [[lilac]], [[lavender]] and [[mauve]], but is greyer than each of them [5]. The swatch is dusty and slightly warm, a lilac that has been dulled [5]. Paterson's classified index places heather among the blues, which shows how loosely the word is pinned to one hue [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The name appears in Maerz and Paul (1930) and the ISCC-NBS system (1955) [5]. It is rare in painting: 4 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, as photographed, and only 1 within the painting measure [7]. In printed English the color adjective peaks in the 1890s, while the word in all senses peaks in 2010 [7].

questions.q: What did heather mean as a word before the twentieth century, according to St Clair?
True or false: heather is a bright, saturated purple.

openers: Heather once meant mottled; the color is a speckle of small purple flowers, not a flat tone.
